title: Usama ibn Munqidh's memoirs
hook: a Syrian knight's memoir of the Crusades, curious and human
tomorrow: a sick poet, a dream, a cloak. what did he write when he woke?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Biruni set out other people's beliefs as they are, before any argument. Today, a knight tries something like it with the people he's fighting.

On the news, a war usually arrives as maps, arrows and one word for the other side. Here's a memoir that doesn't fit that. Usama ibn Munqidh was a Syrian knight who fought the Franks, the Crusaders, for much of his life. Yet in his memoir there's an odd line. When he visits Jerusalem, he describes the Templars, the Frankish knights then holding the al-Aqsa mosque, as his friends. They give him a small place beside it to pray. A knight on one side, calling knights on the other side friends. How does that fit?
screen: `THE WAR AS MAPS AND ARROWS.` → `A KNIGHT WHO FOUGHT THE FRANKS.` → `THE TEMPLARS: "MY FRIENDS"?`

segments.voice: Keep reading and the scene answers it. Usama stands to pray, and a Frank he doesn't know rushes in, grabs him and turns him to face east: this is how you pray. The Templars pull the man away and apologize. He's a stranger, they explain, just arrived from the Frankish lands, and he's never seen anyone pray any other way. Usama turns back and finishes his prayer. Then he writes the moral he drew: the Franks who had lived a while among Muslims behaved better than the newcomers. That's the key to the puzzle. Usama doesn't see an army; he sees people, one at a time. Some he likes, some he mocks, some he can't figure out, and he writes all of them down with a traveler's curiosity. He never stops being on his own side. But his memoir's name, the Book of Learning by Example, tells you what he's after: lessons, not scores. He also writes, as a man who survived many battles, that a life's length is in God's hands: boldness doesn't shorten it, and caution doesn't stretch it. War, for him, is still a place where humans meet. That's a human view of war.
screen: `A NEWCOMER TURNS HIM EAST.` · `THE TEMPLARS APOLOGIZE.` · `PEOPLE, ONE AT A TIME.` · `LESSONS, NOT SCORES.` · then, large: `A HUMAN VIEW OF WAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you mostly know as the other side: a rival team, a neighbor you argue with, a cousin on the far end of every debate. Find one ordinary, human thing about them, the way they laugh, someone they look after. Stay with that one detail.
screen: `SOMEONE FROM THE OTHER SIDE.` · `ONE HUMAN DETAIL.` · `STAY WITH IT.`

segments.voice: Usama ibn Munqidh's memoirs: a Syrian knight's book of the Crusade years, full of curious, frank portraits of friend and foe.
Something for the road: a human view of war, where even across a battle line a face stays a face. Travelers and historians, all eight, complete.

howItsDone: Readers today study Usama ibn Munqidh's memoir as a window on the Crusade years from a Muslim knight's side; teachers use it to show enemies seen as people, curious and complicated.

fork.setup: your school plays its biggest rival. one of their players helps your injured teammate off the field. at the team dinner, everyone trashes their whole school. what fits Usama's memoir?
options: join in. loyalty means you don't praise the other side.
tell the story of that player by name, rivalry and all.
say the rivalry is pointless and you're done with it.
fork.reveal: Usama keeps his side and still writes down the decent people on the other one, by name and by deed.
